solution: Here \(a > 0\) is assumed, since otherwise the limits and the radical \(\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}}\) do not make sense. Put \(x = a \sin \theta\), so that \(dx = a \cos \theta \, d\theta\) and \(\sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}} = a \cos \theta\) (which is non-negative for \(\theta \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\)); the limits \(x = 0, \, x = a\) become \(\theta = 0, \, \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Then \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{a \cos \theta}{a \sin \theta + a \cos \theta} \, d\theta = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos \theta}{\sin \theta + \cos \theta} \, d\theta\). The denominator \(\sin \theta + \cos \theta = \sqrt{2} \, \sin\left(\theta + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\) is strictly positive on \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), so the integrand is continuous and the integral is an ordinary convergent one. Now apply the property \(\int_{0}^{a} f(x) \, dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x) \, dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\); since \(\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \cos \theta\) and \(\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \sin \theta\), we get \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta + \sin \theta} \, d\theta\). Adding the two expressions for \(I\), \(2I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sin \theta + \cos \theta}{\sin \theta + \cos \theta} \, d\theta = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} 1 \, d\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). \(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\), a value independent of \(a\).

First note that the integral is improper at both ends: \(\log \tan x \to -\infty\) as \(x \to 0^{+}\) and \(\log \tan x \to +\infty\) as \(x \to \dfrac{\pi}{2}^{-}\). It nevertheless converges, because near \(0\) we have \(\tan x \approx x\) so \(\left|\log \tan x\right|\) behaves like \(\left|\log x\right|\), and \(\int_{0} \log x \, dx\) converges; the behaviour at \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) is the mirror image of this. So the symmetry argument below is legitimate. Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \tan x \, dx\) and apply the property \(\int_{0}^{a} f(x) \, dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x) \, dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Since \(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) = \cot x = \dfrac{1}{\tan x}\), we get \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \cot x \, dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \left(\dfrac{1}{\tan x}\right) dx = -\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \tan x \, dx = -I\). Hence \(2I = 0\). \(\therefore I = 0\). (The cancellation is genuine and not an artefact: the positive part on \(\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\) and the negative part on \(\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\) are each finite.)

Write the integrand in a form the properties can act on: \(\log\left(\dfrac{1}{x} - 1\right) = \log\left(\dfrac{1 - x}{x}\right)\) for \(0 < x < 1\), where \(\dfrac{1 - x}{x} > 0\) so the logarithm is defined. The integral is improper at both endpoints, but only logarithmically, and \(\int_{0}^{1} \left|\log x\right| dx = 1\) is finite, so \(I = \int_{0}^{1} \log\left(\dfrac{1 - x}{x}\right) dx\) converges. Now use the property \(\int_{0}^{a} f(x) \, dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x) \, dx\) with \(a = 1\). Replacing \(x\) by \(1 - x\) turns \(\dfrac{1 - x}{x}\) into \(\dfrac{x}{1 - x}\), which is the reciprocal, so \(I = \int_{0}^{1} \log\left(\dfrac{x}{1 - x}\right) dx = -\int_{0}^{1} \log\left(\dfrac{1 - x}{x}\right) dx = -I\). Hence \(2I = 0\). \(\therefore I = 0\). Equivalently, \(I = \int_{0}^{1} \log(1 - x) \, dx - \int_{0}^{1} \log x \, dx\), and the same substitution shows the two integrals are equal (each is \(-1\)), so their difference is \(0\).

The denominator is \(1 + \sin x \cos x = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2} \sin 2x\), which on \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) lies between \(1\) and \(\dfrac{3}{2}\) and so never vanishes; the integrand is therefore continuous and the integral is an ordinary one. Let \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sin x - \cos x}{1 + \sin x \cos x} \, dx\) and apply \(\int_{0}^{a} f(x) \, dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x) \, dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Under \(x \mapsto \dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\) we have \(\sin x \mapsto \cos x\) and \(\cos x \mapsto \sin x\), so the product \(\sin x \cos x\) in the denominator is unchanged while the numerator becomes \(\cos x - \sin x\), the negative of the original. Hence \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos x - \sin x}{1 + \sin x \cos x} \, dx = -I\), giving \(2I = 0\). \(\therefore I = 0\).

The integrand \(x^{2} (3 - x)^{5/2}\) is continuous on \([0, 3]\) (the exponent \(\dfrac{5}{2}\) is positive, so nothing blows up at \(x = 3\)). Expanding \((3 - x)^{5/2}\) directly is awkward, so use the property \(\int_{0}^{a} f(x) \, dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x) \, dx\) with \(a = 3\), which swaps the roles of the two factors: \(I = \int_{0}^{3} (3 - x)^{2} \, x^{5/2} \, dx\). Now the bracket is a polynomial and can be expanded: \(I = \int_{0}^{3} \left(9 - 6x + x^{2}\right) x^{5/2} \, dx = \int_{0}^{3} \left(9 x^{5/2} - 6 x^{7/2} + x^{9/2}\right) dx\). Integrating term by term, \(I = \left[9 \cdot \dfrac{2}{7} x^{7/2} - 6 \cdot \dfrac{2}{9} x^{9/2} + \dfrac{2}{11} x^{11/2}\right]_{0}^{3} = \dfrac{18}{7} \cdot 3^{7/2} - \dfrac{4}{3} \cdot 3^{9/2} + \dfrac{2}{11} \cdot 3^{11/2}\). Using \(3^{7/2} = 27\sqrt{3}\), \(3^{9/2} = 81\sqrt{3}\) and \(3^{11/2} = 243\sqrt{3}\), this is \(\dfrac{486}{7}\sqrt{3} - 108\sqrt{3} + \dfrac{486}{11}\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{3}\left(486 \cdot \dfrac{18}{77} - 108\right) = \sqrt{3} \cdot \dfrac{8748 - 8316}{77}\). \(\therefore I = \dfrac{432\sqrt{3}}{77}\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the key gives 8/21, which is the value belonging to Ex 4.2 II (4) — the two keys are swapped. This integral is singular at both limits and converges only as a Cauchy principal value, which is 0 by odd symmetry.]

Let \(f(x) = \dfrac{x^{3}}{9 - x^{2}}\). Then \(f(-x) = \dfrac{(-x)^{3}}{9 - (-x)^{2}} = \dfrac{-x^{3}}{9 - x^{2}} = -f(x)\), so \(f\) is an odd function on the symmetric interval \([-3, 3]\), and the property \(\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) \, dx = 0\) for odd \(f\) gives the book's answer \(I = 0\). An honest warning must accompany this: the integrand is not defined at the endpoints \(x = \pm 3\), where \(9 - x^{2} = 0\), and the singularity is not integrable, because near \(x = 3\) we have \(\dfrac{x^{3}}{(3 - x)(3 + x)} \approx \dfrac{9}{2(3 - x)}\) and \(\int \dfrac{dx}{3 - x}\) diverges. Consequently \(\int_{0}^{3} f\) is \(+\infty\) and \(\int_{-3}^{0} f\) is \(-\infty\), and the integral does not converge in the ordinary sense. What is genuinely zero is the Cauchy principal value \(\lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^{+}} \int_{-3+\varepsilon}^{3-\varepsilon} f(x) \, dx\), which is \(0\) for every \(\varepsilon\) by the odd symmetry. \(\therefore I = 0\), understood as a principal value.

Let \(f(x) = \log\left(\dfrac{2 + \sin x}{2 - \sin x}\right)\). On \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) we have \(\sin x \in [-1, 1]\), so both \(2 + \sin x\) and \(2 - \sin x\) lie in \([1, 3]\) and are strictly positive; the logarithm is therefore defined and \(f\) is continuous on the whole closed interval, so this is an ordinary convergent integral with no singularity to worry about. Since \(\sin(-x) = -\sin x\), \(f(-x) = \log\left(\dfrac{2 - \sin x}{2 + \sin x}\right) = \log\left[\left(\dfrac{2 + \sin x}{2 - \sin x}\right)^{-1}\right] = -f(x)\), so \(f\) is odd. By the property \(\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) \, dx = 0\) when \(f\) is odd, \(\therefore I = 0\).

Split the numerator: \(I = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{x}{2 - \cos 2x} \, dx + \dfrac{\pi}{4} \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{1}{2 - \cos 2x} \, dx\). On this interval \(2x \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), so \(\cos 2x \in [0, 1]\) and \(2 - \cos 2x \in [1, 2]\) is never zero: both integrands are continuous. Since \(\cos 2(-x) = \cos 2x\), the first integrand is (odd) \(\div\) (even) \(=\) odd, so by \(\int_{-a}^{a} (\text{odd}) = 0\) it contributes nothing; the second integrand is even, so \(\int_{-a}^{a} (\text{even}) = 2\int_{0}^{a}\) gives \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \cdot 2 \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{dx}{2 - \cos 2x} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{dx}{2 - \cos 2x}\). Put \(t = 2x\), \(dt = 2 \, dx\): \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{dt}{2 - \cos t}\). Now substitute \(u = \tan \dfrac{t}{2}\), so \(\cos t = \dfrac{1 - u^{2}}{1 + u^{2}}\), \(dt = \dfrac{2 \, du}{1 + u^{2}}\), and \(t = 0, \, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) give \(u = 0, \, 1\). Then \(2 - \cos t = \dfrac{2(1 + u^{2}) - (1 - u^{2})}{1 + u^{2}} = \dfrac{1 + 3u^{2}}{1 + u^{2}}\), so \(\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \dfrac{dt}{2 - \cos t} = \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{2 \, du}{1 + 3u^{2}} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \left[\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt{3} \, u\right)\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}\). Hence \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \cdot \dfrac{2\pi}{3\sqrt{3}}\). \(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi^{2}}{6\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} \, \pi^{2}}{18}\).

Let \(f(x) = x^{3} \sin^{4} x\). Here \(x^{3}\) is odd and \(\sin^{4} x\) is even, because \(\sin(-x) = -\sin x\) and the fourth power kills the sign: \(\sin^{4}(-x) = (-\sin x)^{4} = \sin^{4} x\). A product of an odd function and an even function is odd, so \(f(-x) = -f(x)\). The integrand is a product of polynomials and sines, hence continuous everywhere, so there is no convergence issue on the symmetric interval \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]\). By the property \(\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) \, dx = 0\) for odd \(f\), \(\therefore I = 0\).

[Textbook answer-key error: the key gives 0, but the integrand is strictly positive on the interior so the integral cannot vanish. The value is \((\pi/8)\log 2=0.27220\).]

The integrand \(\dfrac{\log(x + 1)}{x^{2} + 1}\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\), so the integral is an ordinary one. Put \(x = \tan \theta\), so \(dx = \sec^{2}\theta \, d\theta\) and \(x^{2} + 1 = \sec^{2}\theta\); the limits \(x = 0, \, x = 1\) become \(\theta = 0, \, \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Then \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \log(1 + \tan \theta) \, d\theta\). Apply the property \(\int_{0}^{a} f(x) \, dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x) \, dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\). Since \(\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \theta\right) = \dfrac{1 - \tan \theta}{1 + \tan \theta}\), we get \(1 + \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - \theta\right) = 1 + \dfrac{1 - \tan \theta}{1 + \tan \theta} = \dfrac{2}{1 + \tan \theta}\). Hence \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \log\left(\dfrac{2}{1 + \tan \theta}\right) d\theta = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \log 2 \, d\theta - \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \log(1 + \tan \theta) \, d\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \log 2 - I\). Therefore \(2I = \dfrac{\pi}{4} \log 2\). \(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi}{8} \log 2\).

Split the integral as \(I = \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{x^{3}}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 4}} \, dx + \int_{-1}^{1} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 4}} \, dx\); both pieces are continuous on \([-1, 1]\) because \(x^{2} + 4 \geq 4 > 0\), so the splitting is legitimate. In the first piece \(x^{3}\) is odd and \(\sqrt{x^{2} + 4}\) is even, so the quotient is odd and \(\int_{-a}^{a} (\text{odd}) \, dx = 0\) makes it vanish. The second integrand is even, so \(\int_{-a}^{a} (\text{even}) \, dx = 2 \int_{0}^{a}\) gives \(I = 2 \cdot 2 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 4}} = 4 \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 2^{2}}}\). Using \(\int \dfrac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2} + a^{2}}} = \log\left|x + \sqrt{x^{2} + a^{2}}\right| + c\), \(I = 4 \left[\log\left(x + \sqrt{x^{2} + 4}\right)\right]_{0}^{1} = 4 \left[\log\left(1 + \sqrt{5}\right) - \log 2\right]\). \(\therefore I = 4 \log\left(\dfrac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)\).

Let \(f(x) = \dfrac{x + x^{3}}{16 - x^{2}}\). The numerator \(x + x^{3}\) is odd and the denominator \(16 - x^{2}\) is even, so \(f(-x) = \dfrac{-x - x^{3}}{16 - x^{2}} = -f(x)\): \(f\) is odd on the symmetric interval \([-a, a]\), and the property \(\int_{-a}^{a} f(x) \, dx = 0\) for odd \(f\) gives \(I = 0\). This is valid only when \(\left|a\right| < 4\); the book states no restriction on \(a\), but \(16 - x^{2}\) vanishes at \(x = \pm 4\), and near those points \(f(x)\) behaves like a multiple of \(\dfrac{1}{4 - x}\), which is not integrable, so for \(\left|a\right| \geq 4\) the integral does not converge in the ordinary sense and is zero only as a Cauchy principal value (again by the odd symmetry). \(\therefore I = 0\), for \(\left|a\right| < 4\).

The integrand \(t^{2} \sqrt{1 - t}\) is continuous on \([0, 1]\), so this is an ordinary integral. The awkward factor is the radical, and the property \(\int_{0}^{a} f(t) \, dt = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - t) \, dt\) with \(a = 1\) moves the radical onto the simple factor: \(I = \int_{0}^{1} (1 - t)^{2} \sqrt{t} \, dt\). Expanding, \(I = \int_{0}^{1} \left(1 - 2t + t^{2}\right) t^{1/2} \, dt = \int_{0}^{1} \left(t^{1/2} - 2 t^{3/2} + t^{5/2}\right) dt\). Integrating term by term, \(I = \left[\dfrac{2}{3} t^{3/2} - 2 \cdot \dfrac{2}{5} t^{5/2} + \dfrac{2}{7} t^{7/2}\right]_{0}^{1} = \dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac{4}{5} + \dfrac{2}{7}\). Taking \(105\) as the common denominator, \(I = \dfrac{70 - 84 + 30}{105}\). \(\therefore I = \dfrac{16}{105}\).

The integrand is continuous on \([0, \pi]\), so this is an ordinary integral. Because the factor \(x\) is what makes it hard, use the property \(\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(a + b - x) \, dx\) with \(a = 0\) and \(b = \pi\), i.e. replace \(x\) by \(\pi - x\). Since \(\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x\) and \(\cos(\pi - x) = -\cos x\) so that \(\cos^{2}(\pi - x) = \cos^{2} x\), only the factor \(x\) changes: \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi} (\pi - x) \sin x \, \cos^{2} x \, dx\). Adding this to the original, \(2I = \int_{0}^{\pi} \left[x + (\pi - x)\right] \sin x \, \cos^{2} x \, dx = \pi \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x \, \cos^{2} x \, dx\). For the remaining integral put \(u = \cos x\), \(du = -\sin x \, dx\), with \(x = 0, \, \pi\) giving \(u = 1, \, -1\): \(\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x \, \cos^{2} x \, dx = -\int_{1}^{-1} u^{2} \, du = \int_{-1}^{1} u^{2} \, du = \dfrac{2}{3}\). Hence \(2I = \pi \cdot \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). \(\therefore I = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

The integrand is undefined at both endpoints, so convergence must be checked before any property is used. At \(x = 0\) there is a genuine singularity, \(\log x \to -\infty\), but it is only logarithmic and \(\int_{0} \log x \, dx\) converges. At \(x = 1\) the expression is of the form \(\dfrac{0}{0}\); putting \(x = 1 - h\) gives \(\log x \approx -h\) and \(\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} = \sqrt{(1 - x)(1 + x)} \approx \sqrt{2h}\), so the integrand behaves like \(-\sqrt{\dfrac{h}{2}} \to 0\) and is in fact bounded there. Hence \(I\) converges. Put \(x = \sin \theta\), so \(dx = \cos \theta \, d\theta\) and \(\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} = \cos \theta\) (non-negative on \(\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\)); the limits \(x = 0, \, 1\) become \(\theta = 0, \, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \sin \theta \, d\theta\). Call this \(J\). By \(\int_{0}^{a} f(x) \, dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a - x) \, dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), \(J = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \cos \theta \, d\theta\) as well. Adding the two forms, \(2J = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log(\sin \theta \cos \theta) \, d\theta = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log\left(\dfrac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right) d\theta = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \sin 2\theta \, d\theta - \dfrac{\pi}{2} \log 2\). In the first term put \(t = 2\theta\): \(\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \sin 2\theta \, d\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\pi} \log \sin t \, dt\), and since \(\sin(\pi - t) = \sin t\) the graph is symmetric about \(t = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(\int_{0}^{\pi} \log \sin t \, dt = 2 \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \log \sin t \, dt = 2J\); the first term is therefore \(J\). Thus \(2J = J - \dfrac{\pi}{2} \log 2\), giving \(J = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \log 2\). \(\therefore I = -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \log 2\).
